# Installation

PlotNado needs Python 3.12 or newer. Pick the option that matches how you want to use it:

| You want to... | Use |
|---|---|
| Add PlotNado to an existing Python environment | [pip](#install-with-pip) |
| Get the `plotnado` command, Python API, and a Jupyter kernel without managing environments | [uv tool](#install-as-a-tool-with-uv) |
| Skip installing Python or dependencies | [Container](#run-in-a-container) |
| Change PlotNado itself | [Develop from source](#develop-from-source) |

Check any install with:

```bash
plotnado --version
```

## Install with pip

Use this if you want `import plotnado` in your own scripts or notebooks.
Install it into a virtual environment (or an existing Conda environment):

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install plotnado
```

On Windows, activate the environment with `.venv\Scripts\activate`.

Optional extras add support for more data types:

```bash
pip install "plotnado[cooler]"     # Hi-C / cooler and CapCruncher tracks
pip install "plotnado[quantnado]"  # QuantNado tracks
```

To use PlotNado in Jupyter from this environment, also `pip install ipykernel`.

## Install as a tool with uv

Use this if you do not want to manage a Python environment yourself.
It gives you the `plotnado` command and a way to run Python scripts that use the
PlotNado API, with optional Jupyter support.
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) installs PlotNado in its own isolated environment,
and downloads a suitable Python version if needed.

1. Install uv (once):

    ```bash
    # macOS / Linux
    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
    # or, on macOS with Homebrew
    brew install uv
    ```

2. Install PlotNado:

    ```bash
    uv tool install plotnado
    ```

3. If your shell then says `plotnado: command not found`, add uv's tool directory
   to your `PATH` and open a new terminal:

    ```bash
    uv tool update-shell
    ```

Upgrade or remove it later with:

```bash
uv tool upgrade plotnado
uv tool uninstall plotnado
```

To add optional extras, list them in brackets, e.g. `uv tool install "plotnado[cooler]"`.

### Use the Python API

uv keeps a tool in its own environment, so `import plotnado` does not work from
your system Python. Run Python through `plotnado` instead; everything after
`plotnado python` is passed to the interpreter:

```bash
plotnado python my_plot.py          # run a script that does `import plotnado`
plotnado python                     # interactive Python prompt
plotnado python -m my_package.plots # run a module
```

### Use PlotNado in Jupyter (optional)

To use the API in notebooks, add the `notebook` extra and register PlotNado's environment
as a Jupyter kernel once:

```bash
uv tool install --force "plotnado[notebook]"
plotnado kernel install
```

Then pick **PlotNado** as the kernel in Jupyter Lab, Jupyter Notebook, or VS Code.
Re-run it after `uv tool upgrade plotnado` to refresh the version shown in its name, and
remove it with `plotnado kernel uninstall`.

## Run in a container

A ready-made image with PlotNado, Jupyter Lab, and all dependencies is published for
every release on the GitHub Container Registry. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows
(x86-64 and ARM) with [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) or a compatible
runtime such as Podman.

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/alsmith151/plotnado:latest
```

Tags available:

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `latest` | Most recent release |
| `0.3` | Most recent `0.3.x` release |
| `0.3.3` | One exact release; use this for reproducible analyses |

The container works in `/work`. Mount your data directory there with `-v` so PlotNado
can read your files and write plots back to your machine.

### Run CLI commands

Run from the directory that holds your data and template:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work ghcr.io/alsmith151/plotnado:latest \
  plotnado plot template.yaml --region chr1:1,000,000-1,100,000 --output view.png
```

`view.png` appears in your current directory. All paths in the command and in the
template must be **relative** to that directory (or start with `/work/`); paths on
your machine such as `/Users/me/data/x.bw` do not exist inside the container.

To avoid typing the full command every time, define a shell alias:

```bash
alias plotnado='docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work ghcr.io/alsmith151/plotnado:latest plotnado'

plotnado --version
plotnado init sample1.bw sample2.bw peaks.narrowpeak --auto --output template.yaml
plotnado plot template.yaml --region chr1:1,000,000-1,100,000 --output view.png
```

### Use Jupyter Lab

With no command, the container starts Jupyter Lab on port 8888:

```bash
docker run --rm -p 8888:8888 -v "$PWD":/work ghcr.io/alsmith151/plotnado:latest
```

Open <http://localhost:8888> in your browser. Your current directory appears in
the Jupyter file browser, and notebooks you save there stay on your machine.
Stop the server with `Ctrl+C`.

::: {.callout-warning}
Jupyter Lab in the container has no password or token. Anyone who can reach port 8888
can run code as you. On a shared machine or server, bind to localhost only:
`-p 127.0.0.1:8888:8888`.
:::

### File ownership on Linux

On Linux, files written by the container are owned by `root` by default. Run as your own
user to avoid this:

```bash
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD":/work ghcr.io/alsmith151/plotnado:latest \
  plotnado plot template.yaml --region chr1:1,000,000-1,100,000 --output view.png
```

This works for both CLI commands and Jupyter Lab. macOS and Windows (Docker Desktop)
do not need it.

Images up to and including `0.3.3` also need `-e HOME=/tmp` when run with `--user`,
otherwise Jupyter Lab exits on startup.

### HPC clusters (Apptainer / Singularity)

Most clusters do not allow Docker, but Apptainer can run the same image.
It mounts your home and current directories automatically and runs as your user:

```bash
apptainer pull plotnado.sif docker://ghcr.io/alsmith151/plotnado:latest
apptainer exec plotnado.sif plotnado --version
apptainer exec plotnado.sif plotnado plot template.yaml --region chr1:1,000,000-1,100,000 --output view.png
```

With Apptainer, absolute paths on the cluster file system work as normal.

## Develop from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alsmith151/plotnado
cd plotnado
uv sync --extra dev --extra docs
uv run pytest tests/
uv run python examples/run_examples.py
uv run plotnado --help
```

`uv sync --extra dev --extra docs` installs the package, test tools, and documentation
dependencies into the project environment at `.venv`. Prefix commands with `uv run`
to use it.

To build the container locally:

```bash
docker build -t plotnado:dev .
```

## Build docs locally

Requires [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).

```bash
uv sync --extra dev --extra docs
QUARTO_PYTHON=.venv/bin/python quarto render
QUARTO_PYTHON=.venv/bin/python quarto preview
```

The docs use executable Quarto Python cells. Most examples use deterministic in-memory data;
optional cooler, CapCruncher, and QuantNado examples need their corresponding dependencies
and fixture data.
